newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian industry embrace cassava in recession.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian industry embrace cassava in recession.

text.p: Nigeria's economic ills have prompted food companies and some industrial firms to turn increasingly to home-grown cassava as a substitute for imported products.
Industry executives attending a two-day workshop on cassava in the southwestern city of Ibadan this week said some companies had found cassava an adequate replacement for costly, imported wheat.

"You cannot say because the Nigerian economy is bad then you fold your arms and gape at the customers. So we've had to improvise and substitute," Timi Ogunyanwo, spokesman for Temitope Bakery and Catering Services, told Reuters.
Ogunyanwo's company which is 100 percent Nigerian-owned and located in Shagamu in the southwest, produces biscuits, pastries and confectionery.

"Wheat imports are expensive for us. So at all times our biscuits must have 30 percent of high quality cassava flour. And customers say this variety of biscuit is fantastic, so we're set to push out foreign companies producing biscuits."
A tonne of imported wheat flour costs 21,000 naira or more while cassava flour sells for 15,000 naira or less, Ogunyanwo said.
Cassava, grown on the marginal soils of lowland farms in Nigeria's rain forest and the middle belt states, is a staple in most homes of the country's 100 million people.
Nigeria's economy slumped after a rash of strikes and riots followed the annulment by the army of a 1993 election to restore democracy.
Key economic policies introduced since 1995 by military ruler General Sani Abacha have shown the economy to be recovering but with few positive signs of growth yet.

Tony Strawson, the British managing director of Nigerian German Chemicals (formerly Nigerian Hoescht) which produces chemicals and pharmaceutical drugs, told Reuters his company regularly uses cassava starch, flour and chips.

"We have developed special adhesives and textile sizing solutions with cassava starch. And we're currently trying to perfect its use in producing pain-killing tablets," said Strawson, whose company is based in the southwestern town of Ota and is wholly-owned by Nigerians.

Abdulrahaman Alabi, factory manager of NASCO Foods in Jos, central Nigeria, said he would recommend that his company conducts a research on use of cassava and its derivatives to manufacture some of their products.
"We will like to join the bandwagon to produce at minimum costs and gain more customers and profits," Alabi said.
